With things having settled down somewhat, and his eldest daughter Freida getting older, Reb Moshe set his attention to finding her a match. Whether he was in shul, at the beis midrash, or on a business trip, he was constantly on the lookout.

One day, Reb Moshe set out to daven mincha in the shul on the other side of town, on Portugaler street—the street where descendants of Jews who had been expelled from Portugal, like Reb Baruch Batlan, lived. Reb Moshe had decided to daven in this shul, and to come a little early, in order to pay a bikkur cholim visit to Reb Yona Shmuel the Parush.

Reb Yona Shmuel was an old man; so old, that he was even an old man when Reb Moshe was a boy. He was called a parush because he stayed separate from the rest of society; he never left the beis midrash, except to catch a few hours of sleep at night. In the last few years, ever since his wife passed away, Reb Yona Shmuel sold his house and slept in the beis midrash on a bench next to his sefarim.

Reb Yona Shmuel had grown weak in his old age, and wasn’t able to learn as well as he used to. He asked for different yeshiva students to take turns learning at his table, so that he could at least hear the sounds of limmud Torah.

Reb Moshe drew closer, curious to see who Reb Yona Shmuel’s opponent was. He expected to see an older man; perhaps Reb Asher Yehonasan, or one of his former chavrusas from yeshiva. Instead, in the center of the small crowd that had gathered to watch the debate, there was a young man

who had just the beginnings of a red beard sprouting on his chin. Reb Moshe recognized the bachur as nineteen-year-old Kaddish.

Reb Yona Shmuel propped his thin frame up on his elbows and peered over at the Gemara on the table. A bit of color returned to his sallow cheeks as he read the contested words of Tosfos, and he gestured animatedly with a closed fist as explained his view. “You see?!”

Back and forth the two went, pausing briefly for mincha- ma’ariv, and then continuing into the evening. Finally, after several hours, Reb Yona Shmuel had to agree that Kaddish’s understanding of Tosfos was correct.

But here’s what impressed Reb Moshe most of all: Kaddish’s response to his victory. After Reb Yona Shmuel conceded, the young man simply turned back to his Gemara and continued learning. There wasn’t a hint of pride on his face. He just seemed truly happy to have settled what the words of the Tosfos meant.

Kaddish was learning together with his cousin Binyamin, Reb Baruch Batlan’s son. Reb Moshe went over to the two of them and asked them various questions on the subject they were learning. He walked away impressed with both.

On the one hand, Binyamin’s father, Reb Baruch, was a man whom Reb Moshe truly respected. Reb Baruch was a rare case of Torah u’gedula b’makom echad1—a combination of Torah scholarship and great wealth. Though there was one thing

about Reb Baruch that Reb Moshe didn’t like: his devotion to kabbalah and his teacher, this Yoel of Zamoshch.

orphan boy who grew up in the nearby village of Eretz Hachayim. Eretz Hachayim was was populated by a small group of farmers, all of whom studied kabbalah and followed Reb Yoel Baal Shem. Young men in Eretz Hachayim were only officially taught kabbalah at age eighteen. Kaddish, being an advanced student, had started learning just after his sixteenth birthday— soon before he and his widowed mother moved to Posen.

People called the farmers on Eretz Hachayim “the miracle farmers”, because of the miracle stories that came from their produce. It was said that Shmuel Yosef* the tavern-keeper was

able to make four hundred barrels of beer with just one batch of their barley. And Gnesha* the midwife said that she used milk from their cows to cure a baby girl with croup.

The farm’s produce was so famous for its quality and miraculous powers that none of the farmers needed to come into the big city to sell it on market day! Customers would travel to them in order to buy their fruits, vegetables, and grains.

Reb Moshe didn’t place much stock in these rumors of miracles. But he did have to admit that the farmers of Eretz Hachayim were incredibly kind and honest people.

He had heard from a first-hand witness that a fellow from Prague had once offered the farmers a huge sum of money to buy their entire crop. The farmers had refused, because they wanted to continue to offer their produce to the nearby towns, including Posen, at a fair price.

Plus, Reb Moshe had the opportunity to observe Reb Dovid once or twice, when it was Reb Dovid’s turn to sell the farm’s produce at the Posen market. Reb Moshe remembered Reb Dovid to be a serious man— serious about life, and serious about halacha. And though Reb Dovid was known to study kabbalah, he wasn’t as enthusiastic about it all as was his brother, Reb Baruch. By nature, he was a less passionate person, and only occasionally went to visit the Baal Shem in Zamoshch.

And Kaddish himself, Reb Moshe thought, was probably only interested in kabbalah because he lived in his uncle Baruch’s house. Perhaps once Kaddish moved out of that house, things would change. Thus, because of Reb Dovid’s weaker link to kabbalah, Reb Moshe began to lean towards choosing Kaddish for the shidduch. It also helped that—in Reb Moshe’s estimation, at least—Kaddish was more adept at learning than his cousin Binyamin.
